findings.bible: What happens when a frame runs long: 500 ms clamp; ledger correction WP03-ch06-058 'At the default target the 500 ms clamp allows at most 29 updates in one tick, because 30 steps of 166,667 ticks exceed 500 ms by 100 ns.'
findings.target: modules/runtime/src/Game.cpp::Game::MaxElapsedTime (TimeSpan::FromMilliseconds(500.0) = 5,000,000 ticks) and Game::Tick fixed-step loop; Game(): TargetElapsedTime_(TimeSpan(166667L)). 30 x 166,667 = 5,000,010 ticks, i.e. 10 ticks = 1,000 ns over the clamp; 29 steps leave 166,657 ticks, 10 short of a 30th step. The conclusion (29 updates) is right, the stated margin is 10x too small (100 ns is one tick).
findings.site_now: deep-dives/framework/game-time-and-timestep.html#fixed-step: 'Because 30 steps of 166,667 ticks exceed 500 ms by 100 ns, the clamp allows at most 29 updates...'. Same page #hysteresis-trace labels the six-step row 'One stall of 100 ms or more', but six steps need 6 x 166,667 = 1,000,002 ticks = 100.0002 ms, so exactly 100.0 ms (with no carry-over) gives five steps.

fix.old_html: • Because 30 steps of 166,667 ticks exceed 500 ms by 100 ns, the clamp allows at most 29 updates in one tick at the default target.
fix.html: • Because 30 steps of 166,667 ticks are 5,000,010 ticks, 10 ticks (1 µs) more than the 5,000,000 ticks of the 500 ms clamp, the clamp allows at most 29 updates in one tick at the default target.

fix.old_html: One stall of 100 ms or more
fix.html: One stall of about 100 ms or more (six steps need 100.0002 ms)

findings.target: modules/runtime/src/Game.cpp::Game::PollEvents calls GraphicsDevice_.GetRenderer().DebugSimulateContextLoss()/DebugRestoreContext() with no try/catch; modules/renderers/webgpu/src/WebGPURenderer.cpp::WebGPURenderer::DebugSimulateContextLoss throws System::NotSupportedException while unrecoverableResourceCount_ > 0 (TextureCube, RenderTargetCube, Texture3D, occlusion query, custom ShaderEffect); DirectX11Renderer/DirectX12Renderer/WebGPURenderer set deviceLost_ so CanBeginDrawEXT() is false until DebugRestoreContext(). Game::Run catches std::exception, logs and rethrows; EmscriptenMainLoopCallback catches, logs and clears the loop slot.
findings.site_now: deep-dives/framework/game-class-and-lifecycle.html#debug-keys: '... WebGPU families declare non-empty overrides ..., so on those renderers the keys really rehearse a loss and a recovery.' The page has no mention that a lone F9 stops drawing on D3D11/D3D12/WebGPU or that WebGPU F9 can throw out of Run(); that is only on known-issues/bugs/cna-bug-078.html#actual, which the Game page does not link. The exception-boundary section of the same page also says nothing about this route to main(), and development/debugging.html#black ('Rule out the debug hotkeys', the natural place for a black-window cause) says only that a family 'implements' the seam.

fix.old_html: so on those renderers the keys really rehearse a loss and a recovery. What each family does is renderer-specific;
fix.html: so on those renderers the keys rehearse a loss and a recovery, with two consequences that are easy to miss. On DirectX 11, DirectX 12 and WebGPU a lone F9 marks the device lost and, with a registered GraphicsDeviceManager, BeginDraw() then refuses every frame until F10 restores it, so the game keeps updating but stops drawing. On WebGPU, F9 also throws System::NotSupportedException while a TextureCube, RenderTargetCube, Texture3D, occlusion query or custom ShaderEffect is alive, and nothing in PollEvents, Tick or Run catches it: natively it propagates out of Run() after the logged “fatal exception” line, and in the browser loop it is logged and the loop stops without raising Exiting (CNA-BUG-078). XNA's Game reserves no keys at all. What each family does is renderer-specific;

fix.old_html: A game that binds either key also triggers the renderer's context-loss seam where a family implements it.
fix.html: A game that binds either key also triggers the renderer's context-loss seam where a family implements it. On DirectX 11, DirectX 12 and WebGPU a lone F9 makes BeginDraw() refuse every frame (with a registered GraphicsDeviceManager) until F10 restores the device, which looks like a frozen or black window while Update keeps running; on WebGPU with a TextureCube, RenderTargetCube, Texture3D, occlusion query or custom ShaderEffect alive, F9 throws System::NotSupportedException instead (CNA-BUG-078).

findings.bible: What this buys a porting engineer: 'A Game subclass that only used the public, documented XNA surface ... should port to CNA by translating syntax, not by redesigning its structure.'
findings.target: Public XNA members whose behaviour differs at TARGET: Game::setInactiveSleepTimeProperty (stored, never applied; XNA Tick sleeps), Game::ResetElapsedTime (no-op under fixed step; XNA sets the flag in both modes), Game::Tick IsRunningSlowly lag counter (XNA: two counters, <20 ticks), GameComponent::Dispose(bool) (no Components.Remove; XNA removes), DrawableGameComponent::Initialize (no device-service events; XNA hooks four), Game::ShowMissingRequirementMessage (never called); all confirmed above against the XNA decompile (Game.cs, GameComponent.cs, DrawableGameComponent.cs).
findings.site_now: deep-dives/framework/game-class-and-lifecycle.html#porting keeps 'ports by translating syntax' as the headline and then files InactiveSleepTime and ShowMissingRequirementMessage under 'XNA internals or behaviour the framework performs implicitly', although both are public XNA surface; the other public-surface divergences documented in the sibling deep dives (ResetElapsedTime, IsRunningSlowly, component disposal, DrawableGameComponent events) are absent from the checklist.

fix.old_html: • A game class that uses only the public XNA surface of Game ports by translating syntax: the same virtuals, the same event names, the same timing and component properties under get…Property() spellings.
fix.html: • A game class that uses only the public XNA surface of Game ports by translating syntax: the same virtuals, the same event names, the same timing and component properties under get…Property() spellings. The names carry over; the behaviour is not guaranteed to be identical, and the differences listed next are on that public surface.

fix.old_html: • Code that depended on XNA internals or on behaviour the framework performs implicitly needs a second look: ShowMissingRequirementMessage is never called, InactiveSleepTime is not applied, IsActive is false under RunOneFrame(), and the browser loop swallows frame exceptions.
fix.html: • Public members whose behaviour differs from XNA 4.0 need a second look: ShowMissingRequirementMessage is never called, InactiveSleepTime is not applied, ResetElapsedTime() does nothing under the fixed step, IsRunningSlowly follows a different rule (GameTime and the timestep), a DrawableGameComponent loads once and does not follow the device, disposing a GameComponent does not remove it from Components (components). Also check IsActive under RunOneFrame() (false) and the browser loop, which swallows frame exceptions.

findings.bible: IsRunningSlowly: five-tick hysteresis (ledger: a single tick with six or more updates sets it; a 50 ms stutter never does) and the XNA-parity claims about the timestep modes.
findings.target: modules/runtime/src/Game.cpp::Game::Tick: updateFrameLag_ += max(0, stepCount-1); flag set only when updateFrameLag_ >= 5, cleared only at 0. Three updates in one tick (a 50 ms hitch) never set it. XNA 4.0 (decompiled Game.Tick) uses two counters and a <20 tick window, ResetElapsedTime differs, InactiveSleepTime is applied by XNA but not by CNA, and the Emscripten body has its own clock, so 'exactly' is not supportable.
findings.site_now: docs/game-loop.html: (a) #fixed-vs-variable-timestep says 'CNA replicates the XNA timestep modes exactly.'; (b) the IsFixedTimeStep row says the framework calls Update() multiple times 'if the GPU fell behind, setting getIsRunningSlowlyProperty() to true in that case'; (c) the GameTime table row says the flag is set 'when fixed-timestep logic is behind schedule and has had to run multiple Update() calls in a single frame'. All three contradict the new #isrunningslowly-rule subsection on the same page and the GameTime-and-timestep deep dive (tutorials 05, 48 and 73 were already aligned).

fix.old_html: CNA replicates the XNA timestep modes exactly. The default is fixed timestep.
fix.html: CNA offers XNA's two timestep modes and, on the native loop, XNA's own clock rules (with the fixed step a zero-length first update; in both modes TotalGameTime advancing only after Update returns). It does not replicate XNA exactly: IsRunningSlowly follows a different rule, ResetElapsedTime() does nothing under the fixed step, InactiveSleepTime is stored but never applied, and the browser loop keeps its own clock (see the Emscripten caveat below and GameTime and the timestep). The default is fixed timestep.

fix.old_html: calls Update() multiple times per render frame if the GPU fell behind, setting getIsRunningSlowlyProperty() to true in that case.
fix.html: calls Update() multiple times per render frame if the frame ran long. getIsRunningSlowlyProperty() turns true only once the accumulated catch-up lag reaches five extra steps (how it is decided).

fix.old_html: Set to true by the framework when fixed-timestep logic is behind schedule and has had to run multiple Update() calls in a single frame to catch up.
fix.html: Set to true by the framework once the fixed-timestep loop's accumulated catch-up lag reaches five extra Update() steps: a single 50 ms hitch (three updates) never sets it, while a stall of about 100 ms or more does at once (see How IsRunningSlowly is decided).

findings.bible: Explicit disposal, destructor cleanup, and the gap between them (Dispose(true) vs Dispose(false) do different work).
findings.target: modules/runtime/src/Game.cpp::Game::Dispose(bool): only the disposing==true branch disposes components, Content_ and the graphics device service; ~Game calls Dispose(false), which only sets isDisposed_.
findings.site_now: docs/game-loop.html#disposebool says 'In C++ the distinction is less significant than in C#, but the method is present for full XNA compatibility.' while the h3 directly below (#dispose-false-path, added by the audit) says 'In CNA the disposing flag decides almost everything.' The two sentences on the same page contradict each other.

fix.old_html: In C++ the distinction is less significant than in C#, but the method is present for full XNA compatibility.
fix.html: In CNA the distinction still decides which cleanup runs (see below): only the true path disposes components, the content manager and the device service.

findings.bible: Vertical retrace ...: 'XNA's third public choice, PresentInterval::Two, cannot be expressed through this Boolean ... SDL Renderer and EasyGL submit the numeric 2 but cannot guarantee driver acceptance; D3D9 has a literal native interval 2 but it is fullscreen- and capability-dependent. Several other products reduce every positive value to ordinary VSync.'
findings.target: modules/renderers/vulkan/src/VulkanRenderer.cpp::CreateSwapchain (swapInterval_ == 2 selects FIFO_RELAXED, else FIFO); modules/renderers/metal/src/MetalRenderer.mm::SetSwapInterval (displaySyncEnabled = (i != 0), so 2 behaves as 1); the full per-family table is on deep-dives/renderers/presentation-and-backbuffer-readback.html#swap-interval.
findings.site_now: deep-dives/framework/game-time-and-timestep.html#present-interval-two says only that 'whether the driver honours it is renderer- and platform-specific and should be checked on the target renderer'. That hides that on several families CNA itself, not the driver, decides (Vulkan: FIFO_RELAXED, not half-rate; Metal: any nonzero is ordinary vsync), and the page never links the cross-renderer swap-interval table that preserves the Bible's specifics.

fix.old_html: whether the driver honours it is renderer- and platform-specific and should be checked on the target renderer.
fix.html: whether it means half-refresh presentation is renderer-specific, and on several families CNA itself decides rather than the driver: Vulkan maps 2 to FIFO_RELAXED, which is not half-rate presentation, and Metal treats any nonzero interval as ordinary display sync. A game that needs 30 Hz pacing should therefore not rely on Two; use TargetElapsedTime. The family-by-family results are tabulated on Presentation modes, swap interval, native handles and back-buffer readback; check the target renderer.

findings.bible: The override points: 'During initialization, Game subscribes [UnloadContent] to the registered graphics-device service's DeviceDisposing event' (Game::Initialize is where the base does its framework work, including calling LoadContent).
findings.target: modules/runtime/src/Game.cpp::Game::Initialize initialises Components_ by index, caches the IGraphicsDeviceService, subscribes UnloadContent to DeviceDisposing and then calls LoadContent() (or defers it to DeviceCreated); Game::DoInitialize calls Initialize() first, then clears and rebuilds the ordered lists from Components_, and only afterwards subscribes ComponentAdded/ComponentRemoved. A component added after the base Initialize() returns (still inside the derived Initialize) is therefore categorised, updated and drawn but never has Initialize() called.
findings.site_now: docs/game-loop.html: the lifecycle list says 'Initialize() - non-content game setup; call Game::Initialize() at the top' and lists LoadContent() as a separate later step; the Initialize section says it runs 'before any content is loaded'; the LoadContent section says it is called 'immediately after Initialize()'. The page never says that the base Initialize() itself calls LoadContent(), and 'at the top' contradicts the page's own example (components registered before the base call) and Tutorial 04 / Tutorial 08 / the Game-class deep dive, which state that LoadContent runs inside Game::Initialize().

fix.old_html: • Initialize() — non-content game setup; call Game::Initialize() at the top (once)
fix.html: • Initialize() — non-content game setup; register components and anything LoadContent() depends on before calling Game::Initialize(), which initialises the components and then runs LoadContent() (once)

fix.old_html: Initialize() is called once after the graphics device has been created but before any content is loaded. Use it for non-content setup:
fix.html: Initialize() is called once after the graphics device has been created. Content loading starts when your override calls Game::Initialize(), which initialises the registered components and then calls LoadContent(); anything LoadContent() needs, and every component you add, must therefore be in place before that call (a component added after it is updated and drawn but never has its Initialize() called). Use it for non-content setup:

fix.old_html: LoadContent() is called once, immediately after Initialize().
fix.html: LoadContent() is called once, from inside Game::Initialize() (after it has initialised the components), so it runs at the point where your Initialize() override calls the base method.

findings.bible: Composition and interpolation: 'The retained executable quaternion_vs_matrix_demo.cpp compares a Z-axis matrix rotation with the corresponding axis-angle quaternion route ... the matrix components, transformed point, and rendered image agreed.' Dropped as HISTORICAL ONLY (WP04-ch07-059) with the note that 'the equivalence it demonstrated is stated from source on the conventions page (#quaternion-order)'.
findings.target: modules/math/src/Matrix.cpp::Matrix::CreateFromQuaternion and ::CreateRotationX/Y/Z; modules/math/src/Quaternion.cpp::Quaternion::CreateFromAxisAngle. For q = CreateFromAxisAngle(UnitZ, a) = (0, 0, sin(a/2), cos(a/2)): M11 = 1 - 2z^2 = cos a, M12 = 2zw = sin a, M21 = -sin a, M22 = cos a, identical to CreateRotationZ(a); the same holds for X (M22,M23,M32,M33) and Y (M11,M13,M31,M33). CreateFromAxisAngle does not normalise its axis.
findings.site_now: deep-dives/framework/math-coordinate-conventions.html#quaternion-order states only the product-order equivalence CreateFromQuaternion(q1*q2) == CreateFromQuaternion(q2)*CreateFromQuaternion(q1); no page says that a positive axis-angle rotation turns the same way as CreateRotationX/Y/Z, or that the axis is not normalised (site-wide search for CreateRotationZ next to CreateFromAxisAngle finds nothing). The artifact was historic, the behaviour it demonstrated is current.

fix.old_html: Both the matrix and the quaternion default constructors produce all zeros, not the identity: use Matrix::getIdentityProperty() or Quaternion::Identity.
fix.html:
Both the matrix and the quaternion default constructors produce all zeros, not the identity: use Matrix::getIdentityProperty() or Quaternion::Identity.

The single-axis routes agree, so a positive angle turns the same way on both: Matrix::CreateFromQuaternion(Quaternion::CreateFromAxisAngle(Vector3::UnitZ, a)) has the same M11, M12, M21 and M22 as Matrix::CreateRotationZ(a) (cos a, sin a, −sin a, cos a), and likewise about X and Y. CreateFromAxisAngle does not normalise its axis, so pass a unit vector.

findings.bible: Integer geometry and Color: 'Its numeric packed form is AABBGGRR; on little-endian systems the four packed bytes appear as RGBA.' (ledger WP04-ch07-079)
findings.target: modules/math/include/Microsoft/Xna/Framework/Color.hpp::Color::packedValue ('value = AABBGGRR', R in bits 0-7); modules/math/tests/Microsoft/Xna/Framework/ColorTests.cpp::ColorTest.RedPackedValueIsAabbggrr (Color::Red packs to 0xFF0000FF; little-endian memory order R,G,B,A).
findings.site_now: docs/math-types.html (Color table, getPackedValueProperty row): 'The packed 32-bit RGBA value (ABGR in memory on little-endian)'. That is backwards: ABGR is the numeric reading (high byte first); in memory on a little-endian machine the bytes are R, G, B, A. It contradicts deep-dives/framework/rectangle-point-and-color.html#color-layout and development/internals/modules/math.html#colour, which state the layout correctly.

fix.old_html: The packed 32-bit RGBA value (ABGR in memory on little-endian)
fix.html: The packed 32-bit word, numerically AABBGGRR (R in bits 0–7, A in bits 24–31); on a little-endian machine its bytes lie in memory as R, G, B, A. See Rectangle, Point and Color.
